OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Colombia. She alleges that she fears returning to Colombia after being targeted by a guerilla group, the ELN, who targeted her for extortion and demanded payment in order to allow her to continue operating her business. She alleges that when she did not pay the extortion, the ELN threatened to kill her, prompting her to flee to Canada and seek protection.

The Appellant appeals, arguing that the RPD erred in finding that she has a viable IFA.

[8] The Appellant's explanation that she was unaware of the possibility of obtaining such a report to present to the RPD is insufficient to justify its admission as new evidence on appeal. The Appellant was put on notice by the RPD that IFA was a live issue in her claim. She was represented by counsel before the RPD and had the opportunity to present evidence about the viability of the IFA to the RPD. I note that the RPD decision was not made until approximately one month after the hearing, and there is no indication that attempts were made to seek out or submit additional evidence before the decision was made.

[9] It is established in jurisprudence that the purpose of new evidence at the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is not to provide an opportunity for claimants to supplement a deficient record before the RPD. As stated by the Federal Court:
...the Applicant must put her best foot forward before the RPD, and present all the evidence that is available at the time, whether aware of it or not, unless there is an aspect of injustice arising from unexpected new facts, or old facts that no reasonable amount of due diligence could have turned up. It is not intended to be a tune-up procedure for the RAD that upon learning [of] deficiencies in the Applicant's case, additional evidence that could have been presented to the RPD may be presented as new evidence before the RAD."3

[10] For those reasons, I find that this report is inadmissible under s.110(4) and I reject it as new evidence.

Further, according to jurisprudence, I must also find that the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.1

[9] It is established in jurisprudence that the purpose of new evidence at the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is not to provide an opportunity for claimants to supplement a deficient record before the RPD. As stated by the Federal Court:
...the Applicant must put her best foot forward before the RPD, and present all the evidence that is available at the time, whether aware of it or not, unless there is an aspect of injustice arising from unexpected new facts, or old facts that no reasonable amount of due diligence could have turned up. [13] The RPD found that the determinative issue in the Appellant's claim was the availability of a viable IFA in Barranquilla. The panel found that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution from the ELN in Barranquilla, and that it would not be objectively unreasonable for her to relocate there, in consideration of her personal circumstances.

[14] The Federal Court has confirmed that there is a two-pronged test for evaluating the viability of a proposed IFA as follows,5 modified to take account of section 97 of the IRPA:
1. The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA.
2. Conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.

[15] Once an IFA is proposed, the onus is on the claimant to establish that the proposed IFA fails to meet one or both prongs of the test.6

[16] Following my independent review and analysis of the record and arguments before me, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Barranquilla, for the reasons outlined below.
The Appellant has a safe IFA in Barranquilla
The RPD's findings

[17] The RPD considered the means and motivation of the ELN to seek out the Appellant in the proposed IFA in its analysis of the first prong of the IFA test. The panel found that while the ELN has the capacity to locate targets, the objective evidence suggests that they may not have a presence in Atlántico, the region where the IFA is located, and even if they do have a presence there, it is not a strong area of ELN influence or control. The panel further noted that the objective evidence indicates that criminal groups such as the ELN are more likely to track individuals with certain profiles, while the Appellant does not fit into any of these profiles.

[18] The RPD further found that the ELN does not appear to be motivated to seek out the Appellant. The panel noted that the ELN did not seek her out when she relocated to Popayan, a city in another region of Colombia, to avoid them in 2016, notwithstanding that Popayan is in a stronghold ELN territory.

[19] The RPD noted that the Appellant's adult children still live in Popayan and have not been pursued by the ELN, despite that the ELN made specific threats to the lives of the Appellant's family if she did not cooperate with their extortion demand. The RPD further considered the Appellant's allegation that the ELN had killed her brother in XXXX 2020, but found that there was insufficient evidence to establish that her brother was killed by the ELN.

[20] Finally, the RPD noted that the motivation for the ELN's extortion, which was a demand for a payment in order to allow the Appellant to continue operating her business, has ceased, as her business is no longer in operation.

[21] In view of the above factors, the RPD concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the ELN has the means and motivation to seek out the Appellant in the proposed IFA.
The Appellant's arguments

[22] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its analysis of the safety of the proposed IFA. She submits that the objective evidence indicates that the ELN has a presence in the Atlántico region and in major cities, thus establishing their presence in Barranquilla, a major city which is located in Atlántico. She submits that the evidence that the ELN is more likely to target individuals with particular profiles does not mean that they are unlikely to pursue her, and argues that the RPD's finding in this regard is an unreasonable plausibility finding.

[23] The Appellant further argues that the fact that the ELN did not pursue her in Popayan in 2016 does not establish that they lack the motivation to pursue her "debt" of monies "owed" to them. She submits that it is speculative to assume that they are no longer interested in pursuing her for the purpose of retaliating for her failure to comply with their extortion demands, and that it is speculative to assume that illegal armed groups always or even usually approach family members of a target.
The RAD's analysis

[24] I find that the RPD correctly found that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the ELN has the motivation to pursue the Appellant if she relocates to the proposed IFA in Barranquilla.

[25] The RPD did not make plausibility findings about the means and motivation of the ELN to seek out the Appellant, and I reject the Appellant's arguments in that regard. As noted in the jurisprudence cited by the Appellant, plausibility findings relate to the credibility of alleged facts or events that are alleged by a claimant to have taken place. A finding that a sworn allegation is not credible because it is not plausible may only be made in the clearest of cases such as when "the facts as presented are outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected, or where the documentary evidence demonstrates that the events could not have happened in the manner asserted by the claimant."7

argument_evidence.context_text: [26] In the present case, the RPD was not assessing the credibility of facts or past events alleged by the Appellant; rather, the panel was assessing the evidence in the record to determine whether it is sufficient to establish a particular risk threshold or likelihood of the ELN pursuing the Appellant in the proposed IFA in the future.

[26] In the present case, the RPD was not assessing the credibility of facts or past events alleged by the Appellant; rather, the panel was assessing the evidence in the record to determine whether it is sufficient to establish a particular risk threshold or likelihood of the ELN pursuing the Appellant in the proposed IFA in the future.
[27] Having reviewed the evidence, I agree with the RPD that it does not establish that the Appellant faces such a risk.

[28] Even accepting that the ELN has a presence in Barranquilla, and accepting that the Appellant could be a potential target despite not falling into the profiles of individuals commonly targeted by such groups as outlined in the objective evidence, I find that the behaviour of the agents of harm does not suggest that they are motivated to pursue the Appellant in the proposed IFA in connection with their past extortion attempt.

[28] Even accepting that the ELN has a presence in Barranquilla, and accepting that the Appellant could be a potential target despite not falling into the profiles of individuals commonly targeted by such groups as outlined in the objective evidence, I find that the behaviour of the agents of harm does not suggest that they are motivated to pursue the Appellant in the proposed IFA in connection with their past extortion attempt.

[29] While it may not be reasonable to conclude that a group like the ELN would seek out the family members of a target in most or all cases, in this case, the ELN specifically threatened that they would seek out and harm the Appellant's family in retaliation for her failure to pay the extortion money.

[30] Further, the Appellant has not disputed the RPD's finding that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the death of her brother was instigated by the ELN, and I agree with the RPD that there is insufficient evidence to link the Appellant's brother's death to her own problems with the ELN, for the same reasons given by the RPD.

While the Appellant stated both in her Basis of Claim (BOC) and her testimony that the ELN demanded the extortion money in exchange for allowing her to continue operating her business in their territory,8 the Appellant is no longer operating her business.

[32] In consideration that the Appellant is not a high-profile target of the ELN as outlined in the objective evidence,9 that her children continue to live in an ELN stronghold and have not been threatened or found despite the ELN threatening to retaliate against them, that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Appellant's brother's death is linked to the ELN, and that the business that the ELN was trying to extort no longer exists, I find that the evidence does not establish that the Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution, or a risk of section 97 harm on a balance of probabilities, from the ELN in Barranquilla.

[33] Having found that the proposed IFA meets the first prong of the jurisprudential test, I now turn to the second prong of reasonableness.

[34] The RPD noted that the Appellant did not raise any objections to the proposed IFA in respect of the second prong of the test, but nevertheless considered the Appellant's circumstances in analyzing the reasonableness of the proposed IFA. The RPD considered the factors of language, religion, education and employment, housing, and friends and family, and concluded that while the Appellant may face some hardship in relocating, it does not rise to the level to render the IFA as unreasonable.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Colombia. She alleges that she fears returning to Colombia after being targeted by a guerilla group, the ELN, who targeted her for extortion and demanded payment in order to allow her to continue operating her business. She alleges that when she did not pay the extortion, the ELN threatened to kill her, prompting her to flee to Canada and seek protection.

[2] The Appellant's claim was heard before the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on September 23, 2021, and rejected on October 18, 2021, on the grounds that she has a safe and reasonable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Barranquilla, Colombia. The Appellant appeals, arguing that the RPD erred in finding that she has a viable IFA.

[3] Following my review of the evidence and arguments before me, I find that the determinative issue in this appeal is IFA, and I find that the RPD correctly found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Barranquilla.
DECISION

[4] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
NEW EVIDENCE
The new evidence submitted by the Appellant is rejected

[5] According to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I can only accept evidence that arose after the RPD decision, that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision, or that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to be brought to the RPD before the decision. Further, according to jurisprudence, I must also find that the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.1

[6] The Appellant has submitted a report from XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXin XXXX, Colombia Reports,2 dated XXXX XXXX, 2021, after the RPD decision. The report offers an opinion as to the viability of an IFA for the Appellant in the face of her prospective risk of harm from the ELN. The Appellant submits that she could not have been reasonably expected to produce this evidence to the RPD because it responds to the RPD's unreasonable and incorrect findings regarding the ability and motivation of the agents of harm to target the Appellant in the proposed IFA.

[7] I reject this argument, and I find that the Appellant has not established that this evidence is admissible under s.110(4). Though the report is dated after the RPD decision, it refers to events and circumstances which predate the RPD decision and relies entirely on source documents which predate the RPD decision. Further, I find that the Appellant has not established that such a report was not available to her prior to the RPD decision or that she could not have reasonably been expected to produce such evidence to the RPD.

[8] The Appellant's explanation that she was unaware of the possibility of obtaining such a report to present to the RPD is insufficient to justify its admission as new evidence on appeal. The Appellant was put on notice by the RPD that IFA was a live issue in her claim. She was represented by counsel before the RPD and had the opportunity to present evidence about the viability of the IFA to the RPD. I note that the RPD decision was not made until approximately one month after the hearing, and there is no indication that attempts were made to seek out or submit additional evidence before the decision was made.

[9] It is established in jurisprudence that the purpose of new evidence at the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is not to provide an opportunity for claimants to supplement a deficient record before the RPD. As stated by the Federal Court:
...the Applicant must put her best foot forward before the RPD, and present all the evidence that is available at the time, whether aware of it or not, unless there is an aspect of injustice arising from unexpected new facts, or old facts that no reasonable amount of due diligence could have turned up. It is not intended to be a tune-up procedure for the RAD that upon learning [of] deficiencies in the Applicant's case, additional evidence that could have been presented to the RPD may be presented as new evidence before the RAD."3

[10] For those reasons, I find that this report is inadmissible under s.110(4) and I reject it as new evidence.
There will be no oral hearing

[11] Subsection 110(6) of the IRPA provides that the RAD may hold an oral hearing if new evidence is accepted that raises a serious credibility issue with respect to the Appellant, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee claim, and if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the claim. As no new evidence was admitted, the RAD will proceed without an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS
[12] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.4

[13] The RPD found that the determinative issue in the Appellant's claim was the availability of a viable IFA in Barranquilla. The panel found that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution from the ELN in Barranquilla, and that it would not be objectively unreasonable for her to relocate there, in consideration of her personal circumstances.

[14] The Federal Court has confirmed that there is a two-pronged test for evaluating the viability of a proposed IFA as follows,5 modified to take account of section 97 of the IRPA:
1. The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA.
2. Conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.
[15] Once an IFA is proposed, the onus is on the claimant to establish that the proposed IFA fails to meet one or both prongs of the test.6

[16] Following my independent review and analysis of the record and arguments before me, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Barranquilla, for the reasons outlined below.
The Appellant has a safe IFA in Barranquilla
The RPD's findings

[17] The RPD considered the means and motivation of the ELN to seek out the Appellant in the proposed IFA in its analysis of the first prong of the IFA test. The panel found that while the ELN has the capacity to locate targets, the objective evidence suggests that they may not have a presence in Atlántico, the region where the IFA is located, and even if they do have a presence there, it is not a strong area of ELN influence or control. The panel further noted that the objective evidence indicates that criminal groups such as the ELN are more likely to track individuals with certain profiles, while the Appellant does not fit into any of these profiles.

[18] The RPD further found that the ELN does not appear to be motivated to seek out the Appellant. [20] Finally, the RPD noted that the motivation for the ELN's extortion, which was a demand for a payment in order to allow the Appellant to continue operating her business, has ceased, as her business is no longer in operation.

[21] In view of the above factors, the RPD concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the ELN has the means and motivation to seek out the Appellant in the proposed IFA.

[22] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its analysis of the safety of the proposed IFA. She submits that the objective evidence indicates that the ELN has a presence in the Atlántico region and in major cities, thus establishing their presence in Barranquilla, a major city which is located in Atlántico. The RAD's analysis
[24] I find that the RPD correctly found that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the ELN has the motivation to pursue the Appellant if she relocates to the proposed IFA in Barranquilla.

[25] The RPD did not make plausibility findings about the means and motivation of the ELN to seek out the Appellant, and I reject the Appellant's arguments in that regard. As noted in the jurisprudence cited by the Appellant, plausibility findings relate to the credibility of alleged facts or events that are alleged by a claimant to have taken place. A finding that a sworn allegation is not credible because it is not plausible may only be made in the clearest of cases such as when "the facts as presented are outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected, or where the documentary evidence demonstrates that the events could not have happened in the manner asserted by the claimant."7

[26] In the present case, the RPD was not assessing the credibility of facts or past events alleged by the Appellant; rather, the panel was assessing the evidence in the record to determine whether it is sufficient to establish a particular risk threshold or likelihood of the ELN pursuing the Appellant in the proposed IFA in the future. It is not a matter of whether it is plausible that the ELN could pursue the Appellant in the IFA; but of whether the evidence in the record establishes that the Appellant would face a risk that amounts to a serious possibility of persecution, or a section 97 risk of harm in the IFA on a balance of probabilities, in the IFA location.
[27] Having reviewed the evidence, I agree with the RPD that it does not establish that the Appellant faces such a risk.

[28] Even accepting that the ELN has a presence in Barranquilla, and accepting that the Appellant could be a potential target despite not falling into the profiles of individuals commonly targeted by such groups as outlined in the objective evidence, I find that the behaviour of the agents of harm does not suggest that they are motivated to pursue the Appellant in the proposed IFA in connection with their past extortion attempt.

[29] While it may not be reasonable to conclude that a group like the ELN would seek out the family members of a target in most or all cases, in this case, the ELN specifically threatened that they would seek out and harm the Appellant's family in retaliation for her failure to pay the extortion money. Those family members continue to live undisturbed in ELN territory. As such, I find that their failure to pursue the family members, or to pursue the Appellant through her family members, is indicative of their lack of ongoing motivation and interest in the Appellant.

[30] Further, the Appellant has not disputed the RPD's finding that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the death of her brother was instigated by the ELN, and I agree with the RPD that there is insufficient evidence to link the Appellant's brother's death to her own problems with the ELN, for the same reasons given by the RPD.

[31] I also agree with the RPD that the fact that the motivation behind the extortion no longer exists is a relevant consideration. While the Appellant stated both in her Basis of Claim (BOC) and her testimony that the ELN demanded the extortion money in exchange for allowing her to continue operating her business in their territory,8 the Appellant is no longer operating her business.

[32] In consideration that the Appellant is not a high-profile target of the ELN as outlined in the objective evidence,9 that her children continue to live in an ELN stronghold and have not been threatened or found despite the ELN threatening to retaliate against them, that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Appellant's brother's death is linked to the ELN, and that the business that the ELN was trying to extort no longer exists, I find that the evidence does not establish that the Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution, or a risk of section 97 harm on a balance of probabilities, from the ELN in Barranquilla.
The proposed IFA is reasonable
[33] Having found that the proposed IFA meets the first prong of the jurisprudential test, I now turn to the second prong of reasonableness.

[34] The RPD noted that the Appellant did not raise any objections to the proposed IFA in respect of the second prong of the test, but nevertheless considered the Appellant's circumstances in analyzing the reasonableness of the proposed IFA. The RPD considered the factors of language, religion, education and employment, housing, and friends and family, and concluded that while the Appellant may face some hardship in relocating, it does not rise to the level to render the IFA as unreasonable.

[35] The Appellant has not disputed the RPD's findings on the second prong. I agree with the RPD, for the reasons it gave, that the evidence does not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Barranquilla, in consideration of all of the circumstances.
CONCLUSION
[36] The RPD correctly determined that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Barranquilla.

[37] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
